title: Quantum extreme learning for forecasting experimental chaotic electronic circuits
authors: Mohammad Sharifian, Qingyu Li, Chiranjib Mukhopadhyay, Abolfazl Bayat, Ludovico Minati
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing and its special case, quantum extreme learning, are powerful tools for predicting classical discrete time-series with quantum devices. Forecasting continuous signals, however, requires careful discretization as oversampling artificially boosts short-term accuracy but fails over realistic intervals, while undersampling captures too few features and yields poor predictions. Here, we experimentally generate four continuous time-series signals from a chaotic electronic circuit for forecasting with quantum extreme learning. Since simplified circuit models do not fully capture real behaviour, it is unclear whether algorithms that predict simulated time-series also work for experimental signals. We address discretization via two approaches: (i) sampling local peaks/troughs; and (ii) uniform sampling at the autocorrelation timescale. The former captures resonant behaviour, while the latter fully captures chaotic features as well as allowing the reconstruction of chaotic attractors. Our algorithm achieves high forecasting accuracy for both simulated and experimental signals, demonstrating its power for continuous signal processing on near-term quantum simulators, and remains robust against moderate decoherence.
summary: This work applies Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL) to forecast continuous time-series data generated by chaotic electronic circuits. It tackles the critical issue of discretizing continuous signals using two specialized sampling methods. The results show that QEL successfully predicts these complex dynamics, proving its utility for processing real-world, non-linear physical measurements on near-term quantum simulators.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of forecasting continuous time-series signals, particularly those exhibiting chaotic behavior, using quantum computing devices.
main_result: The Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL) algorithm achieves high forecasting accuracy for both simulated and experimental chaotic signals, demonstrating robustness against moderate decoherence.
method: The method involves encoding classical time-series data into quantum states, evolving these states under a quantum Hamiltonian, and then using linear regression on the measurement expectation values for prediction.
model_or_system: The system utilizes an experimental chaotic electronic circuit generating four continuous signals, and the quantum model employs an open nearest-neighbor XYZ spin chain Hamiltonian for evolution.
key_observables: Forecasting accuracy quantified by Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) for four signals ($u_{C1}, u_{C2}, i_{L1}, i_{L2}$); autocorrelation function $R[k]$.
important_parameters: Discretization lag ($m$) determined by the $1/e$ crossing of the autocorrelation function; quantum evolution time $	au$; number of steps ($N_{steps}$) and hidden qubits ($N_{hid}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the QEL framework can effectively map continuous chaotic dynamics onto quantum measurements, and the discretization method must be carefully chosen (peak/trough vs. autocorrelation timescale).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic framework of QEL (encoding, evolution, readout) and show the oscillator circuit topology and experimental setup.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of continuous signal forecasting, details the QEL protocol (encoding, evolution via Hamiltonian, readout), discusses two discretization approaches (maplike and uniform), and validates the method using both simulated and real experimental chaotic circuit data.
why_interesting: The application of quantum machine learning techniques (QEL) to model and predict complex, non-linear, and chaotic dynamics from physical circuits provides a novel bridge between quantum computation and condensed matter/classical physics modeling.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic overview of the proposed framework. The experimental electronic chaos generator produces four signals, uC1, uC2, iL1, and iL2, which are discretized using a sampling lag m determined from the first 1/e crossing of the autocorrelation function of each signal. Selected past samples, separated by this lag, are encoded into qubits through rotation encoding, while the remaining Nhid qubits remain in |0⟩. All qubits evolve under the reservoir Hamiltonian H for a time τ, followed by measurements of the local Pauli expectation values. The resulting measurement vector is used to train the linear readout and to predict the signal values.

The gray curves represent the actual continuous signals, while the triangles and circles represent the true and predicted extrema, respectively.
